title: Mstislav Rostropovich
wiki_lead:
Mstislav Leopoldovich Rostropovich (27 March 1927 – 27 April 2007) was a Soviet and Russian cellist and conductor. In addition to his interpretations and technique, he was well known for both inspiring and commissioning new works, which enlarged the cello repertoire more than any cellist before or since. He inspired and premiered over 100 pieces, forming long-standing friendships and artistic partnerships with composers including Dmitri Shostakovich, Sergei Prokofiev, Nikolai Myaskovsky, Henri Dutilleux, Witold Lutosławski, Olivier Messiaen, Luciano Berio, Krzysztof Penderecki, Alfred Schnittke, Norbert Moret, Andreas Makris, Leonard Bernstein, Aram Khachaturian, and Benjamin Britten.
Rostropovich was internationally recognized as a staunch advocate of human rights, and was awarded the 1974 Award of the International League of Human Rights. He was married to the soprano Galina Vishnevskaya and had two daughters, Olga and Elena Rostropovich. He received numerous accolades, including a Polar Music Prize.

He was married to the soprano Galina Vishnevskaya and had two daughters, Olga and Elena Rostropovich. He received numerous accolades, including a Polar Music Prize.


Early years

Mstislav Rostropovich was born in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR, to parents who had moved from Orenburg in Russia: Leopold Vitoldovich Rostropovich, a renowned cellist and former student of Pablo Casals, and Sofiya Nikolaevna Fedotova-Rostropovich, a talented pianist. Leopold (1892–1942) was born in Voronezh to Witold Rostropowicz, a composer of Polish noble descent with distant Belarusian roots, and Matilda Rostropovich (née Pule) of German and Huguenot descent. The Polish part of his family bore the Bogoria coat of arms, which was located at the family palace in Skotniki.
Mstislav's mother, Sofiya Fedotova, of Russian descent, was the daughter of musicians and herself a conservatory-trained pianist. Her elder sister, Nadezhda, married cellist Semyon Kozolupov, who was thus Rostropovich's uncle by marriage.
Rostropovich grew up in Baku and spent his youth there. During World War II his family moved back to Orenburg and then, in 1943, to Moscow.
At age four, Rostropovich began studying piano with his mother. He began learning the cello at age eight from his father. In 1943, at age 16, he entered the Moscow Conservatory, where he studied cello with his uncle Semyon Kozolupov, piano with Nikolai Kuvshinnikov, and composition with Vissarion Shebalin. His teachers also included Dmitri Shostakovich. In 1945, he came to prominence as a cellist when he won the gold medal in the Soviet Union's first ever competition for young musicians. He graduated from the Conservatory in 1948 and became professor of cello there in 1956.


First concerts

Rostropovich gave his first cello concert in 1942. He won first prize at the International Music Awards of Prague and Budapest in 1947, 1949 and 1950. In 1950, at age 23, he was awarded what was then considered the highest distinction in the Soviet Union, the Stalin Prize. At that time, Rostropovich was already well known in his country and, while actively pursuing his solo career, taught at the Leningrad Conservatory and the Moscow Conservatory. In 1955, he married Galina Vishnevskaya, a leading soprano at the Bolshoi Theatre.
Rostropovich had working relationships with Soviet composers of the era. Nikolai Myaskovsky dedicated his Cello Sonata no. 2, Op. 81, to Rostropovich, and they premiered it together in 1949. Inspired by the performance, Sergei Prokofiev wrote his own Cello Sonata, Op. 119, for Rostropovich, who gave its first performance in 1950 with Sviatoslav Richter. Prokofiev also dedicated his Symphony-Concerto to him; it premiered in 1952. Rostropovich and Dmitry Kabalevsky completed Prokofiev's Cello Concertino after the composer's death. Shostakovich wrote both his first and second cello concertos for Rostropovich, who also gave their first performances.

grok_lead: Mstislav Leopoldovich Rostropovich (27 March 1927 â 27 April 2007) was a Soviet-born Russian virtuoso cellist and conductor, celebrated for his profound interpretations of the standard cello repertoire and premieres of contemporary works dedicated to him by composers such as Dmitri Shostakovich and Benjamin Britten. Born in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR, to musician parents, Rostropovich demonstrated prodigious talent from childhood, studying cello under his father and later at the Moscow Conservatory, where he graduated with top honors and began performing internationally in the 1940s. His career in the Soviet Union included principal roles at the Bolshoi Theatre and extensive recordings, but mounting tensions with authorities over artistic freedom culminated in 1974 when, after sheltering dissident author Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn and publicly criticizing censorship in an open letter to Pravda, he and his wife, soprano Galina Vishnevskaya, were stripped of Soviet citizenship and forced into exile. In the West, Rostropovich rebuilt his career, serving as music director of the National Symphony Orchestra in Washington, D.C., from 1977 to 1994, during which he elevated the ensemble's profile through rigorous standards and innovative programming. His advocacy extended beyond music; he championed human rights, performed at the Berlin Wall in 1989 symbolizing the fall of communism, and received numerous accolades including the Presidential Medal of Freedom and Russia's Order of Merit for the Fatherland. Citizenship was restored in 1990, allowing his return to Russia, where he continued conducting until health declined, dying in Moscow from liver cancer.
